134.title: Purim: gifts and noise
134.hook: food for friends, gifts for the poor, and noise to drown out Haman's name
134.howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the megillah read twice, making noise at Haman's name, send mishloach manot of at least two foods to a friend, give gifts to at least two poor people, and share a festive meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the megillah, the scroll of Esther, where God's name never appears. Your line was hidden, not absent. Did you catch something quietly going right? Day one hundred thirty-four.

Imagine sitting in a synagogue while someone reads a long story aloud from a scroll, and every time one particular name comes up, the whole room explodes. Kids spin wooden rattlers that sound like a flock of angry ducks. Adults stamp their feet. Someone bangs two pot lids together. The reader stops, waits for the noise to die down, and carries on, until the name comes up again. The name is Haman. And the next morning, doorbells ring all over the neighborhood: kids in costumes, holding little baskets of cookies and candy, delivering them door to door.
screen: `A NAME, AND THE ROOM EXPLODES.` → `RATTLERS AND POT LIDS.` → `BASKETS AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: At the end of the book of Esther, Mordecai writes to the Jews and tells them how to keep these days forever: as "days of feasting and gladness, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor." From that one verse come the practices of Purim. Sending portions: in Hebrew, mishloach manot. Jewish law says to send at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food to at least one friend. People make whole projects of it: baskets, themes, the triangle-shaped cookies called hamantaschen. Gifts to the poor: matanot la-evyonim, money or food for at least two people in need, given on the day itself, so they can celebrate too. A festive meal in the afternoon. And hearing the megillah read, evening and morning. The noise comes from an old custom of blotting out the name of Amalek, the ancient enemy the rabbis linked to Haman. The rattle is called a grogger, from Yiddish. Now here's the teaching that changes how the whole day feels. The great twelfth-century teacher Maimonides wrote that it's better to spend more on gifts to the poor than on your own feast or on gifts to friends. Why? Because, he says, there's no greater joy than gladdening the hearts of the poor, the orphans, the widows and the strangers. The person who does that is like the Divine Presence. So Purim's joy is built in two directions at once: toward your friends, and toward people who might have nothing to celebrate with. Happiness on this day isn't complete until it's shared.
screen: `FEASTING, PORTIONS, GIFTS TO THE POOR.` · `TWO FOODS TO A FRIEND.` · `NOISE TO BLOT OUT A NAME.` · `MORE FOR THE POOR THAN THE FEAST.` · then, large: `SENDING PORTIONS ONE TO ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send someone a small food gift. Something simple: two things, a piece of fruit and a cookie, left at a door or handed over at work. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of a friend who'd be surprised by it. Then think of someone who has less than you. See both of them in your mind. Decide on one small thing for each. The bell holds the time.
Mishloach manot. Sending portions: gifts of food to friends on Purim, alongside gifts to the poor.
Your line: give on the happy day. The next time you're celebrating something, share a piece of it with someone who isn't. Day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: Passover: the seder
135.hook: a meal in order, with matzah, bitter herbs, four cups and a story told to children
135.howItsDone: On the first night of Passover (and outside Israel, often the second too), Jewish families hold a seder: reading the Haggadah, drinking four cups, eating matzah and bitter herbs, and answering children's questions, including the four questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mishloach manot: food for friends on Purim, and gifts to the poor. Your line was give on the happy day. A month after Purim, the spring festival arrives. Day one hundred thirty-five.

It's the first night of Passover. The table is set for more people than usual, with extra chairs borrowed from the neighbors. There's a plate with strange things on it: a roasted bone, a bitter root, a sweet brown paste, a sprig of green, salt water. There's flat, crackly bread under a cloth. Everyone has a book in front of them. And before the main meal is served, which may be a long time from now, the youngest child at the table stands up, maybe a little nervous, and asks a question everyone has been waiting for: why is this night different from all other nights?
screen: `EXTRA CHAIRS, A STRANGE PLATE.` → `FLAT BREAD UNDER A CLOTH.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: This meal is the seder. The word means order, because the evening follows fixed steps, each with a name, from the first blessing over wine to the songs at the end. The book on the table is the Haggadah, which means the telling. Because at its heart, the seder is a story told out loud. The Torah commands it: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." Notice: for me. Not for my ancestors. The Haggadah says each person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Everything on the table helps tell it. Matzah, the flat bread, because they left in such a hurry the dough had no time to rise. Maror, bitter herbs, for the bitterness of slavery. Charoset, the sweet paste, looking like the mortar they used for bricks. Salt water, for tears. Four cups of wine, which the rabbis link to four promises of redemption in the book of Exodus. And the questions. The whole night is built to make children ask. There are the four questions. There are four children in the Haggadah, the wise one, the rebellious one, the simple one, and the one who doesn't know how to ask, and each gets an answer suited to them. Food is hidden so kids will hunt for it. The rabbis even say: if there's no child, an adult asks. And if you're all alone at the seder, you ask yourself. A freedom that doesn't ask questions, the seder seems to say, isn't finished yet.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one real question at dinner. Not how was your day. A real one. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'll eat with next, or talk to next. What have you never asked them? Where they came from. What they were afraid of as a kid. What they'd want to be free of. Choose one question and hold it ready. The bell holds the time.
Seder. Order: the Passover meal, told in fixed steps, where the story of leaving Egypt is passed on through food and questions.
Your line: ask the questions. Tonight, at dinner or on the phone, ask one person one question you've never asked them, and really listen. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: Counting the Omer (Leviticus 23:15–16)
136.hook: forty-nine days counted from Passover to Shavuot
136.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover, many Jews count the Omer each night after dark: a blessing, then the day and week (today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer), for forty-nine nights until Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seder: a meal in order, built so children will ask. Your line was ask the questions. What did you ask, and what did you hear? The seder is only the first night. Day one hundred thirty-six.

After dark on the second night of Passover, someone stands, says a short blessing, and then says a number. Today is one day of the Omer. The next night, two days. The night after, three. It goes on like that every night for seven weeks, out loud, a blessing and a number, until forty-nine. Nothing is crossed off, and nothing is skipped. A sentence that takes ten seconds to say, and a household that has to remember it forty-nine nights in a row. And if someone forgets a night, there's a rule for that too.
screen: `A BLESSING, THEN A NUMBER.` → `EVERY NIGHT FOR SEVEN WEEKS.` → `AND A RULE FOR FORGETTING.`

segments.voice: It comes from the Torah: "And ye shall count unto you" from the day the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to the priest, "seven weeks shall there be complete," and then the fiftieth day is a festival. That first sheaf was called the omer. An omer is a measure of grain, and it gives the whole period its name: the Omer, and the practice, counting the Omer. Passover falls at the barley harvest. Seven weeks later comes the wheat harvest and the holiday of Shavuot. So the count ties two harvests together. Over time, the rabbis also saw it tying two events together: leaving Egypt, and receiving the Torah at Sinai. Leaving slavery, and then receiving a way to live. The count is the road between them. The way it's done is precise. Each night after dark, you say a blessing and then the number: today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer. You say it, not just think it. You count up. If you forget to count one night, you can count the next day, without the blessing. But if you miss a whole day, the Shulchan Aruch rules that you keep counting every night, just without the blessing, because the chain was broken. The weeks have a sadder side too. Tradition remembers that many of Rabbi Akiva's students died in this season, so some communities keep signs of mourning, like no weddings, until the thirty-third day, called Lag BaOmer, which is a day of bonfires and joy. In kabbalah, each of the forty-nine days is linked to its own quality to work on, so each day is worth something by itself.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS SHALL THERE BE COMPLETE.` · `OMER: A SHEAF OF BARLEY.` · `FROM EGYPT TO SINAI.` · `SAY THE NUMBER OUT LOUD.` · then, large: `EACH DAY COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count one day tonight. Before that, settle, and breathe. Count your breaths up, slowly: one, two, three, up to seven, and start again. Don't rush to the end; there isn't one. Notice that each breath is complete in itself. Then think of something you're in the middle of. What day of it is this? Say the number to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Omer. A sheaf of barley, and the forty-nine days counted aloud, night by night, from Passover to Shavuot.
Your line: count the days up. Tonight, say out loud what day you're on in something you've started: a habit, a recovery, a new job. Day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: Shavuot
137.hook: the day the Torah was given, kept with all-night study and the book of Ruth
137.howItsDone: On Shavuot, many Jews stay up all night studying Torah (Tikkun Leil Shavuot), pray at dawn, read the Ten Commandments and the book of Ruth in synagogue, and eat dairy foods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Omer: forty-nine nights, counted up out loud. Your line was count the days up. On the fiftieth day, the count arrives. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

It's one in the morning, and the synagogue lights are still on. The room is full, and nobody's praying yet. They're studying. Pairs of people bent over books, arguing gently. A teacher at the front with a room of teenagers. Someone's brought a thermos of coffee and a plate of cheesecake. A few people are dozing on the benches. They'll stay like this until the sky starts to lighten, and then pray the morning service at dawn. On this night, staying awake is the whole point.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `A ROOM FULL OF STUDY.` → `AWAKE UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: The holiday is Shavuot, which means weeks: the seven weeks just counted. In the Torah itself, Shavuot is a harvest festival, the day an offering from the new wheat was brought, the day of first fruits. The Torah never says that anything else happened on this day. But the rabbis did the math. The Torah says the Israelites reached Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, and in the Talmud the sages reckon that the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of that month, which is Shavuot; one rabbi says the seventh. So in Jewish tradition, Shavuot became the time of the giving of the Torah. The gift at the mountain. One reason given for the all-night study is a midrash: on the morning the Torah was given, the Israelites overslept, and Moses had to wake them. Later, Jewish mystics made a practice of staying up all night on Shavuot, to be awake this time, and the custom spread. It's called a tikkun, a repair. Then there's Ruth. On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read. It's a harvest story, set during the barley and wheat harvests. And Ruth, a woman from Moab, chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi and join her people, with these words: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." One reason given for reading it today: it's the story of someone freely accepting the Torah, just as Israel did at Sinai. And Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David. There's also a custom of eating dairy foods; the reasons given vary, and no one reason is certain.
screen: `SHAVUOT: WEEKS.` · `A HARVEST, AND THE GIFT AT SINAI.` · `AWAKE ALL NIGHT THIS TIME.` · `RUTH: WHITHER THOU GOEST.` · then, large: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one page late tonight. Something worth staying up for: a psalm, a chapter of Ruth, a page of something wise. For now, settle, and breathe. Think about the gifts you've been given that you almost slept through. A teacher. A conversation. A book someone pressed into your hands. Pick one. Tonight, stay awake a little longer for it. The bell holds the time.
Shavuot. Weeks: the festival fifty days after Passover, a wheat harvest, and the time Jews remember the giving of the Torah.
Your line: stay up for the gift. Tonight, give the last fifteen minutes before sleep to one page that matters, instead of the phone. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

138.title: Tisha B'Av
138.hook: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting on the floor
138.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations and mournful poems (kinot) chanted in dim light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot: a night awake for the gift of the Torah, and Ruth's great promise. Your line was stay up for the gift. Today, the last stop on our walk through the year, and a day of mourning. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

One word, chanted slowly in a dim room: eichah. How. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and in Hebrew it's also the book's name. On this summer night the curtain has been taken off the ark. People aren't in their seats; they're sitting on the floor, or on low stools, some in socks or canvas sneakers. No one greets anyone with a hello. The reader goes on by a small light, verse after verse. The whole room sits low, as if someone has died. In a way, someone has.
screen: `ONE WORD: EICHAH. HOW.` → `THE CURTAIN OFF THE ARK.` → `SITTING ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Tisha B'Av means the ninth of the month of Av. It's a day of mourning. On this date, the Mishnah says, both Temples in Jerusalem were destroyed: the first by Babylon, and the second by Rome. The Mishnah adds other sorrows to the same date, and over the centuries, later tragedies were remembered on it too, among them, by later tradition, the expulsion of the Jews from Spain. So Tisha B'Av became the day to mourn many losses at once. It's kept like a day of mourning for a close relative. A fast, from sunset to nightfall, like Yom Kippur. No leather shoes. No washing for pleasure. And people sit on the floor or low stools, the way mourners do in the week after a funeral. Then the book of Lamentations is read, five short poems of grief over Jerusalem. It opens: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" Even Torah study, usually a joy, is limited to sad texts. Still, the day isn't only despair. The rabbis asked why the Second Temple fell, and answered: baseless hatred, people hating each other for nothing. So the day becomes a call to repair how people treat each other. At midday, mourners may rise from the floor. And there's an old tradition that on Tisha B'Av, of all days, the redeemer is born. And near its end, Lamentations pleads to begin again: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." When the book is read aloud, that verse is said again after the last one, so the reading ends on it. And that closes our walk through the year: the calendar and the moon, the new year and the fast, the booth, the lights, the trees, the scroll, the seder, the count, the gift, and today, the floor.
screen: `TISHA B'AV: THE NINTH OF AV.` · `BOTH TEMPLES, AND LATER SORROWS.` · `SITTING LOW, LIKE A MOURNER.` · `BASELESS HATRED, AND A HOPE.` · then, large: `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit on the floor for five minutes. You can start now. If it's comfortable for you, lower yourself to the floor; if not, sit low in a chair. Settle, and breathe. Think of one loss you carry, big or small. You don't have to fix it or explain it. Just let the ground hold you while you hold it. If you pray, you can say the old line from Lamentations: renew our days. The bell holds the time.
Tisha B'Av. The ninth of Av: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting low.
Your line: the floor holds grief. When something is heavy today, sit down low for a minute, and let the ground take some of the weight. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: What tefillin are (Deuteronomy 6:8)
139.hook: two small leather boxes holding Torah passages, bound on arm and head for weekday morning prayer
139.howItsDone: Many Jews put on tefillin each weekday morning for the morning service, binding one box on the upper arm and one on the head, with blessings. They are not worn on Shabbat or major festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tisha B'Av, the last stop on our walk through the year, sitting low with Lamentations. Your line was the floor holds grief. Now we leave the calendar and turn to something worn on the body, every weekday. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

Maybe you've seen it in a photo, or on a street corner, or at an airport gate early in the morning: someone standing quietly, a prayer shawl over their shoulders, a black leather strap wound around their forearm in neat coils, and a small black box sitting right at the top of their forehead. It can look strange if you've never seen it. Even a little severe. But ask the person, and many will tell you it's the most intimate part of their day. For the next five days, we'll open up this one practice, piece by piece.
screen: `A STRAP AROUND THE FOREARM.` → `A BLACK BOX ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `FIVE DAYS, PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: They're called tefillin. The word is usually connected to tefillah, prayer. In English they're sometimes called phylacteries, from a Greek word meaning safeguards, but most Jews just say tefillin. They come from a verse you already know, from the Shema: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." Bind what? The words of God. The rabbis understood the verse literally: write the words down and tie them on. So there are two boxes, each made of black leather, perfectly square, each with a leather strap. One is bound on the arm, one on the head. Inside each box are tiny parchment scrolls, handwritten by a trained scribe with a quill and special ink. They hold four passages from the Torah: two from Exodus, about remembering the Exodus, and two from Deuteronomy, including the Shema itself. So the verse that says bind these words is itself inside the box. In the head box, the four passages are on four separate scrolls, in four compartments. In the arm box, all four are on one scroll, in one compartment. Tefillin are put on for the weekday morning prayer. Not on Shabbat or major festivals, because those days are themselves a sign, the rabbis said, and don't need another. This is old. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, archaeologists found tefillin and their tiny parchments, two thousand years old. And the rabbis taught that tefillin should be treated with great care: never dropped, kept in a bag, and if one falls, many people kiss it when they pick it up.
screen: `TEFILLIN, FROM PRAYER.` · `BIND THEM FOR A SIGN.` · `FOUR PASSAGES, HANDWRITTEN.` · `WEEKDAY MORNINGS, NOT SHABBAT.` · then, large: `FOR A SIGN UPON THY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a thread on your finger to remember. Before that, settle, and breathe. Choose one thing you want to remember all day. A promise. A person. A value. Put it into a few words. Then, if you have a thread or a hair tie or a rubber band, put it on your hand now. If not, press your thumb to one finger. Let the body carry the reminder, so the mind doesn't have to. The bell holds the time.
Tefillin. Two small black leather boxes holding handwritten Torah passages, bound on the arm and the head for weekday morning prayer.
Your line: bind it as a sign. Today, every time you notice the thread on your finger, remember the thing you tied it for. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: The arm and the heart
140.hook: the arm box sits on the upper arm, facing the heart, so action and feeling join
140.howItsDone: When putting on tefillin, the arm box is placed first on the upper weaker arm, angled toward the heart, with a blessing; its strap is then wound around the forearm, usually seven times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tefillin: two small boxes holding the words of the Shema, bound as a sign. Your line was bind it as a sign. Did the thread on your finger remind you? Day one hundred forty.

Try this. Lift your left arm and bend it, like you're about to make a muscle. Now notice where the top of your arm rests: right up against the side of your chest, close to your heart. If you're left-handed, try it on the right. That spot, the soft part of the upper arm just above the elbow, is exactly where the first box goes. And it isn't placed there by accident, or placed just anywhere. It's angled, very slightly, so that when the arm is lowered, the box leans in toward the heart.
screen: `BEND YOUR ARM.` → `IT RESTS BY YOUR HEART.` → `THE BOX LEANS INWARD.`

segments.voice: The arm box is called the shel yad, the one of the hand. The Torah says bind them upon thy hand, and the rabbis read hand here as the upper arm, the muscle that moves the hand. They placed it on the weaker arm, the left for a right-handed person, because the verse's wording hinted at it, and so that the strong hand could do the binding. Then comes the placement. The box sits on the bicep, facing the heart. Why the heart? Because another verse, right beside the command about binding, says: "Therefore shall ye lay up these My words in your heart and in your soul; and ye shall bind them for a sign upon your hand." Heart and hand, in one breath. So the rabbis taught that the box on the arm should be across from the heart, and later teachers draw the lesson: the arm is what you do, the heart is what you feel and want, and this practice ties them together. On this reading, a good feeling that never moves the hand falls short, and so does a deed done without the heart. The arm box is put on first, with a blessing. Then the strap is wound around the forearm, usually seven times, down toward the hand. There's also a tradition that the arm box should be covered, by a sleeve or the prayer shawl, while the head box is visible; one is a private sign, the other a public one. And that's the week: Purim's gifts, the seder's questions, the Omer's count, Shavuot's gift, Tisha B'Av's floor, the boxes, and now the arm against the heart.
screen: `SHEL YAD: THE ONE OF THE HAND.` · `ON THE WEAKER ARM.` · `IN YOUR HEART, UPON YOUR HAND.` · `SEVEN TIMES AROUND THE FOREARM.` · then, large: `HAND AND HEART TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hand on heart before one decision. Try it now. Place one hand flat on your chest. Settle, and breathe. Feel your heartbeat, or just the warmth. Think of one thing you have to decide or do today: a message, a conversation, a purchase. Ask two questions. What do I want to do? What do I actually feel? Wait until they point the same way, or at least until you know where they differ. The bell holds the time.
The arm and the heart. The arm box of tefillin, bound on the upper arm facing the heart, so what we do and what we feel are tied together.
screen: `THE ARM AND THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hand and heart together. Before one decision today, put your hand on your chest for a single breath. Day one hundred forty.
